questions.question: How do bundlers work — webpack vs Vite's dev-server model, and what does the production build do either way?
questions.title: Bundler Models
questions.direct_answer: The bundler problem: browsers need to load your module graph efficiently — bundlers resolve the import DAG, apply transforms (TS/JSX → JS, SASS → CSS), and emit optimized assets. WEBPACK (the classic): bundle EVERYTHING — dev server serves one big bundle (rebuilt incrementally with HMR over a websocket — the patch-in-place reload that keeps state), production = full graph optimization (code splitting via dynamic import(), tree-shaking from ESM static structure, minify, content-hash filenames). VITE (the modern default): dev server serves files NATIVELY — native ESM over HTTP (the browser does the module loading; on-demand transforms of just the modules requested — instant startup, near-instant HMR bounded to the changed module — the DX win), production = Rollup (esbuild-powered) bundle — so you get unbundled dev speed AND an optimized prod artifact. The shared concepts either way: entry, chunk graph, code splitting, tree-shaking, source maps, HMR, plugins.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The two models, side by side:

```text
WEBPACK (bundle-centric):
  dev:    build ONE bundle (incremental + HMR patches it live)
  prod:   resolve DAG → split chunks → tree-shake → minify →
          emit hashed assets + sourcemaps
  strength: mature plugin graph, fine chunk control
  cost:    startup scales with graph size (the thing Vite attacks)

VITE (native-ESM dev + Rollup prod):
  dev:    serve FILES as native ESM — the BROWSER requests modules
          on demand; only requested modules get transformed (esbuild:
          TS/JSX 10-100x faster than js compilers)
          → startup instant; HMR = the one changed module (bounded blast
            radius — edits feel local)
  prod:   Rollup bundle: split, tree-shake, hash — same output class
          as webpack, modern defaults
```

The concepts that transfer between both (the vocabulary): ENTRY (the graph root — webpack entries; Vite's index.html); the DEPENDENCY GRAPH (every import resolved — alias/@, node_modules, asset imports); CODE SPLITTING (dynamic import() creates an async CHUNK — route-level/lazy-section boundaries: the user downloads the dashboard code when they navigate there, not at first paint); TREE-SHAKING (ESM's STATIC structure — `import { a }` proves 'b is unimported' → dropped; CommonJS require is dynamic → cannot be proven, stays — the reason libraries ship ESM builds); SOURCE MAPS (the transformed-code → original mapping — DevTools shows YOUR source while running the bundle); HMR (the dev loop: module replaced in place, state-preserving where the runtime accepts it — React Fast Refresh); PLUGINS/LOADERS (the transform pipeline at every step — the extension model).

The production checklist (what a good build does, name the parts): split by route (and vendor) so pages load their own code; preload the current route's chunk (modulepreload) and lazy the rest; content-hash filenames ([name]-[hash].js — immutable caching, the cache-busting mechanism); minify (terser/esbuild) + targeted syntax (browserslist); and measure — a bundle analyzer (visualize the chunks; the 'why is this 400kb' answer).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SRC[source: TS JSX CSS modules] --> RES[resolve import DAG]
    RES --> W[webpack: transform via loaders, bundle ALL]
    RES --> V[Vite dev: transform ON DEMAND, browser fetches ESM]
    W --> HMRW[HMR patches the bundle]
    V --> HMRV[HMR = the one module — bounded blast radius]
    PROD[production — BOTH paths] --> RP[Rollup or webpack graph opt]
    RP --> CS[split chunks via import()]
    RP --> TS2[tree-shake from static ESM]
    RP --> HASH[content-hash + minify + sourcemaps]
    ESBE[esbuild transforms — 10-100x faster] --> V
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why Vite's dev model is faster (the mechanics worth understanding): webpack's dev startup must resolve and build the WHOLE graph before the first page serves; Vite's server answers module requests as they come — the startup cost is the ENTRY page, not the application. The trade that makes it work: native ESM means hundreds of HTTP requests in dev (fine on localhost; esbuild-transformed on demand; and dep optimization — the pre-bundling of node_modules deps with esbuild into ESM, because some packages ship thousands of tiny modules or CJS that needs wrapping). HMR difference is architectural: webpack's HMR propagates through the bundle's module graph to patch dependents; Vite invalidates the changed module's importers — same idea, but bounded by what the browser actually loaded.

The optimization landscape beyond bundling (the modern production answer): esbuild (the Go-based transformer/minifier — the speed engine inside Vite and increasingly the whole pipeline), Rollup (the output-quality bundler — best tree-shaking, the prod half of Vite), SWC (Rust transformer — the Next.js choice), Turbopack (webpack's successor — Rust, incremental), and Rspack (webpack-compatible API on a fast core — the migration-friendly path). The trend to name: JS-in-JS toolchains replaced by native-language cores with JS config/plugin surfaces.

The unbundled-horizon and its limits (the forward-looking layer): native ESM in the browser + import maps (bare specifier resolution WITHOUT a bundler — the platform absorbing the module-resolution role) already work for dev and some light prod; HTTP/2 multiplexing reduced the many-request penalty that motivated bundling — BUT bundling still wins on: request overhead at scale, tree-shaking (dead code only falls out of a static graph), minified-graph optimization, and the deployment/cache model (hashed bundles). The honest summary for interviews: bundlers are no longer REQUIRED for running modules; they're still how you ship an OPTIMIZED graph — and the dev/prod split (native ESM dev, bundle prod) is exactly that insight operationalized.
